title: Snowflake AI functions and Cortex Search

opening.headline: When data is already in the warehouse, AI is used in two ways at the location where the data exists.
body: Let's say hundreds of thousands of customer inquiries have accumulated in a Snowflake table. If we extract this data, classify it, and summarize it by sending it to external AI services, the pathways data travels and the points requiring management will increase accordingly. The LLM provided by Snowflake is deployed within the Snowflake service boundary, enabling direct invocation from where the data resides.

This course compares the functional approach—invoking a model with a single SQL statement (AI_COMPLETE, AI_CLASSIFY, AI_FILTER, AI_AGG)—with the service-oriented approach that retrieves relevant documents for each query (Cortex Search). It then examines the required permissions for invocation and the refresh intervals for search data, and provides examples to illustrate why large-scale row classification is better suited to the functional approach.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the role of AI functions and Cortex Search service
The uses of functional AI and service-based search can be distinguished.

screens.title: The data is in the warehouse, but AI is outside.
screens.lead: First, let's examine the overhead incurred when data and AI are located in different places. Read on while comparing two processing paths illustrated in the diagram.

visual.alt: A diagram comparing the path extending from the warehouse table to an external AI service, and the path processing within the warehouse using a single SQL statement.
labels: AI_CLASSIFY call within a SELECT statement

paragraphs: Hundreds of millions of customer inquiries are already accumulated in Snowflake tables. If you retrieve the data to send it to an external AI API for classification or summarization, data movement paths are created, and additional points where authentication and authorization must be verified arise.

Snowflake Cortex AI Functions addresses this issue in a different way. The LLMs provided by Snowflake are deployed within the Snowflake service boundary, and model invocations can be made via SQL functions or Python. In other words, instead of sending data to the model, the model invocation is brought into the query where the data resides.

The question that needs to be distinguished here is one: how to use AI in places where data exists. This course distinguishes between a functional approach—where a model is invoked via SQL functions—and a service-oriented approach—where a search endpoint is provided as a service—and establishes criteria for determining which approach is appropriate for specific tasks.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Even with the same AI, applying the same judgment to all rows is a different kind of task from retrieving relevant materials each time a question is posed. At the end of the class, students will be able to choose a method based on this distinction.

screens.outro: Now, if you were to think about it, where would you handle this?

screens.title: If large-scale operations need to be classified using AI, where should they be processed?
screens.lead: When you select one of the three processing modes, the instructor's thought process is displayed. Since no answer is entered yet, first consider which mode suits the task at hand before clicking it.

items.prompt: Method 1: Download the data and call one row at a time from the script
items.answer: Although this is the most familiar approach, when dealing with millions of rows, you must directly manage the number of calls, retries, and the process of reloading results back into tables. Additionally, this creates pathways for data to leave the data warehouse. If the data is already in Snowflake, this approach offers little compelling reason to choose it.

items.prompt: Method 2: Calls it once via SQL within the warehouse
items.answer: When calling AI functions within a SELECT statement, the results are directly appended to columns, and the query engine processes them row by row. This is well-suited for batch processing that applies the same judgment to all rows. The functional approach demonstrated in this course is exactly this.

items.prompt: Method 3: Provide a search service that finds relevant documents each time a query is made.
items.answer: This approach is suited for quickly finding a few relevant documents in response to a single query, rather than bulk classification. A typical example is a customer service chatbot searching manuals for each question. This course's service-oriented approach—namely, Cortex Search.

screens.outro: Now that we have recalled the three call patterns, we will first check them individually by function type.

screens.title: Functional: One SQL line calls a model
screens.lead: Select each tab to see how the input and return types differ for each function. The last two tabs cover the permissions required for the call and the previous guidance from the prior function.

tabs.label: AI_COMPLETE
tabs.body: Generates a response using the selected LLM for a given text string or image. This is a function commonly used for most generative tasks. By providing a model name and a prompt, it returns a response sentence, and options such as `temperature` or `max_tokens` can also be supplied. If the input is a review table, it appends a one-line summary sentence to each row as a new column.

tabs.label: AI_CLASSIFY
tabs.body: Classifies text or images into user-defined categories. A typical example is dividing inquiry content into payment, shipping, and account categories. Since the category list is passed together and the result returns the classification value for the corresponding row, it can be directly appended as a column in the SELECT result.

tabs.label: AI_FILTER
tabs.body: Returns true or false for text or image input. Therefore, it can be used as a condition to filter rows in SELECT, WHERE, and JOIN ON clauses. For example, it can be used as a condition to retain only rows that mention delivery delays in reviews. Unlike AI_CLASSIFY, it returns either TRUE or FALSE.

tabs.label: AI_AGG
tabs.body: Aggregates the entire text column into a natural language instruction, returning a single string that captures insights derived from multiple rows. For example, you could instruct it to describe the most common complaint in the review column. This function can process datasets larger than the model's context window and can indicate when an instruction is ambiguous or when no answer exists in the data, so instructions should be explicitly stated as declarative statements.

tabs.label: Required permissions
tabs.body: To call an AI function, the user must have both the `USE AI FUNCTIONS` account-level permissions and either the `CORTEX_USER` or `AI_FUNCTIONS_USER` database role. `USE AI FUNCTIONS` is granted by default to PUBLIC, making it accessible to all users. To narrow the scope, revoke it from PUBLIC and grant it only to specific roles, and this permission management is handled by the ACCOUNTADMIN role.

tabs.label: Previous notice
tabs.body: Migration guidance directs older functions such as `SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX.COMPLETE` to `AI_*` functions. Some migrations require only a name change, while others require checking arguments or return behavior. Review each function's differences before applying a bulk replacement.

screens.outro: Since we've verified the functional component, let's now examine the service-oriented component that handles searches for each query.

screens.title: Service-based: Cortex Search and Dynamic Table
screens.lead: Please read the following SQL from top to bottom. This describes a flow where target data is prepared in a dynamic table, and then a search service is built upon it to execute queries. You can verify the symptoms when each line's meaning diverges from the right-side explanation.

visual.alt: Flow diagram from original table to dynamic table, search service, and query API.

data.code:
CREATE OR REPLACE DYNAMIC TABLE support_articles
  TARGET_LAG = '30 minutes'
  WAREHOUSE = search_wh
AS
  SELECT article_id, answer_text, product, region
  FROM raw_articles
  WHERE status = 'published';

CREATE OR REPLACE CORTEX SEARCH SERVICE support_search
  ON answer_text
  ATTRIBUTES product, region
  WAREHOUSE = search_wh
  TARGET_LAG = '1 hour'
AS (
  SELECT article_id, answer_text, product, region
  FROM support_articles
);

SELECT SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX.SEARCH_PREVIEW(
  'mydb.public.support_search',
  '{"query": "refund period", "columns": ["answer_text", "product"], "filter": {"@eq": {"region": "KR"}}, "limit": 3}'
);

notes.note: A dynamic table is a table that automatically refreshes its data based on the TARGET_LAG criterion, reflecting query results. In this case, only published documents are selected to maintain the latest status with a delay of 30 minutes or less. Without these rows, the search targets would be manually refreshed, potentially resulting in older documents being searched.

`ON` specifies the text column to search, while `ATTRIBUTES` specifies the column to use for filtering results. A service will not be created if the column is not a text column, and filtering is not possible on columns not listed in ATTRIBUTES.

`WAREHOUSE` is the warehouse used when the service creates and updates indexes, and `TARGET_LAG` is the desired delay between changes in the source and when they are reflected in the service. The service is updated periodically, so changes made just now in the source are not immediately detected.

This is the original query for the service. The search column, attribute column, and response column to be returned must all be included in this query. Columns missing from the query will not appear in the result when requested via the columns parameter.

Once the service is created, a low-latency endpoint is provided, allowing queries via Python API, REST API, and SQL `SEARCH_PREVIEW`. `query` is required, `columns` specifies the return columns, `filter` sets a filter based on the ATTRIBUTES column, and `limit` controls the result count. The default limit is 10. If columns are omitted, only the search columns are returned.

screens.outro: Having examined both structures, let's assess which one is appropriate by applying them to a single example.

screens.title: Case Explanation: Why bulk row classification is suitable for functional programming
screens.lead: The instructor breaks down a step-by-step case study of customer inquiry classification over one month. Select the following arrow to examine the nature of the task and try both approaches.

steps.title: Scenario: Assigning categories to 2 million rows of inquiry data
steps.body: Two million rows of customer inquiries accumulated over one month exist in the table. Each inquiry must be tagged with one of the categories: payment, shipping, or account. The same standard must be applied to all rows, and the result must be stored as new table columns.

steps.title: Step 1 Task Characteristic: Independent, repetitive judgment
steps.body: Each row's evaluation is independent of other rows, and the evaluation criteria are the same across all rows. This type of operation is batch processing. The first step in selecting a processing method is to determine whether it is batch processing or whether it involves searching for specific documents for each query.

steps.title: Step 2 Functionally Typed Substitution: Insert AI_CLASSIFY into the SELECT statement
steps.body: When AI_CLASSIFY is included in a SELECT statement and category lists are passed, the classification results are directly attached as columns. Since the query engine processes data row by row, there's no need to manually create calls, retries, or loads. In this case, a functional approach is appropriate.

steps.title: Stage 3 service-based substitution: Search service does not match
steps.body: A search service is structured to quickly return a few relevant documents in response to a single query. To assign classifications to all 200,000 rows, one would need to submit a query for each row, which is not the purpose of search. A service-based approach is not suitable for this task.

steps.title: 4-step counterexample: Manual search of counseling chatbot
steps.body: This time, let's assume that the consultation chatbot needs to find relevant manuals for each question. The questions may arrive at any time, each requiring different documents, and responses must be fast. In this case, Cortex Search is the right solution. The chatbot can use a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) architecture, where it passes search results to an LLM to generate responses.

steps.title: Step 5: Operational Verification: Permissions and Refresh Cycles
steps.body: Before using a function-based approach, verify that the calling privilege `USE AI FUNCTIONS` and a database role are assigned. Before using a service-based approach, confirm that the refresh cycle `TARGET_LAG` for original data changes aligns with business requirements. In both approaches, the review must extend beyond "what is created" to include "who can invoke it and how up-to-date it is."

screens.outro: Finally, let's examine the call permission in more detail.

screens.title: Review before finalization: Permissions and model access scope
screens.lead: When you select the underlined portion in the following command, a description appears explaining what that portion specifies. Pay attention to the order of narrowing privileges.

marks.note: Account-level permissions are managed by the ACCOUNTADMIN role. This command cannot be executed by any other role.

marks.span: REVOKE USE AI FUNCTIONS ON ACCOUNT FROM ROLE PUBLIC
marks.note: By default, revoke the permissions granted to PUBLIC. This prevents users from using most AI functions. However, if a user has only the USE AI FUNCTIONS privilege and does not have the CORTEX_USER role, they can still use AI_AGG and AI_SUMMARIZE_AGG.

marks.span: GRANT USE AI FUNCTIONS ON ACCOUNT TO ROLE analyst
marks.note: Grant permissions only to the required roles. With these permissions, the role can invoke all Cortex AI functions. To make a call, the CORTEX_USER or AI_FUNCTIONS_USER database role must also be present.

marks.span: GRANT USE AI FUNCTION AI_COMPLETE ON ACCOUNT TO ROLE support_bot
marks.note: This form allows control at the function unit level. Only the AI_COMPLETE role can perform this function. Since both comprehensive permissions and function-specific permissions are combined using an OR relationship, a role with comprehensive permissions can continue to invoke all functions even if it revokes specific function permissions.

screens.outro: Having verified the permissions, I will now summarize all the content in one go and conclude.

screens.title: Key Takeaway: Bulk operations are functional; query searches are service-oriented.
screens.lead: This summarizes the two approaches discussed in class. As you read each paragraph, compare your work to determine which category it falls into.

paragraphs: Functional is a way to invoke AI functions such as `AI_COMPLETE`, `AI_CLASSIFY`, `AI_FILTER`, and `AI_AGG` within SQL. Since the results are directly attached to columns or conditions, it is well-suited for batch classification, summarization, and filtering that applies the same judgment to all rows. It is also an advantage that data is not extracted outside of the data warehouse.

Service-based solutions are exemplified by Cortex Search. It provides a hybrid search approach combining vector and keyword search for text data, allowing users to avoid directly managing embedding, infrastructure, and index updates. It is used as the RAG engine for LLM chatbots, the backend search functionality for application search bars, and the search layer for agents. Original changes are reflected every `TARGET_LAG` cycle, so the design must account for the fact that the system will not always be up to date.

Regardless of the method, you must verify the caller's permissions. An AI function must have both the `USE AI FUNCTIONS` account privileges and database roles to be invoked, and if necessary, roles granted from PUBLIC should be revoked and assigned only to specific roles. Remember to first assess the nature of the operation, then select the appropriate method, and finally verify the permissions and up-to-date status.

callout.label: Judgment criteria
callout.text: If the same judgment must be applied to every row, choose a functional approach; if you need to search several relevant documents for each question, choose a service-oriented approach.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: For 2 million rows of customer inquiries over a one-month period, categories must be assigned using the same criteria. What would be the most appropriate choice?
options: Creates Cortex Search service to perform queries per row
Downloads data and makes a single call to an external API.
Call AI_CLASSIFY within SELECT to attach it as a column.
Only creates a dynamic table and handles the classification.
checks.explain: Batch processing that repeatedly applies independent, identical judgments per row is better suited to SQL functional programming, and the AI_CLASSIFY result is directly appended to the column.

wrong.0: Search service is structured to find relevant documents for a single query and does not align with the overall classification of operations.
wrong.1: Exposing data externally increases the number of movement paths and management points.
wrong.3: A dynamic table is a table that periodically refreshes its results, not a model that performs classification.

checks.intro: Pair situations with appropriate methods and organize them. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: Pair up situations with appropriate methods.
left: The consultation chatbot must find relevant manuals for each question.
The review text must be filtered by a WHERE clause based on specific conditions.
The entire text column must be aggregated with a natural language instruction.
checks.explain: Query search is Cortex Search, truth/false determination is AI_FILTER, aggregation is AI_AGG, and general generation is AI_COMPLETE.

glossary.def: AI_A SQL function prefixed with an identifier that enables model invocations to be performed within SQL queries in Snowflake.
A function that evaluates text or image input as true or false and uses it as a condition in WHERE or JOIN clauses.
A feature that provides a hybrid search combining text vectors and keywords, delivered as a service without requiring index management.
This is the target latency allowed for changes in the original data to be reflected in search services or dynamic tables.
This is a table that automatically refreshes based on the delay criteria set for the query results.

misconceptions.myth: AI functions are always accessible to any user.
misconceptions.fact: To call AI functions, both the USE AI FUNCTIONS account privilege and either the CORTEX_USER or AI_FUNCTIONS_USER database role are required. The default privileges granted to PUBLIC may be revoked.

misconceptions.myth: Once a search service is created, you can perform large-scale data classification.
misconceptions.fact: Service-based approach finds relevant documents for a single query. Bulk classification, applying the same judgment to all rows, is better suited to functions like AI_CLASSIFY.

misconceptions.myth: Once Cortex Search is created, original changes are immediately searchable.
misconceptions.fact: The service is updated according to the period specified in TARGET_LAG. The recently changed original may be reflected in the search results after the lag has passed.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Bulk processing that repeats the same judgment across all rows is a functional operation, while the task of finding relevant documents for each query is a service-oriented operation.
Functional calls a model with a single SQL statement, and the result is directly attached as a column or condition.
The service-based approach provides a search endpoint without embedding or index management and is updated periodically with TARGET_LAG.
Account permissions and database roles are both required for AI function calls.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What tasks are performed en masse and what queries involve searches for each case, and which approach is appropriate?
